Senator Ingwersen, Chair Representative Meyer, Chair Members, Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services 100 State House Station Augusta, ME 04333-0100

Re: LD 1583 - An Act Regarding Home Health Care and Hospice Services Ordered by a Health Care Provider Outside of Maine

Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services, thank you for the opportunity to provide information in opposition to LD 1583, An Act Regarding Home Health Care and Hospice Services Ordered by a Health Care Provider Outside of Maine.

This bill allows a home health care or hospice provider to deliver home health care or hospice services to a patient who resides in this State based upon an order from a health care provider from another state or jurisdiction in the United States who is licensed and prescribes services pursuant to an in-person physical examination in the jurisdiction of licensure.

Under CMS regulations at 42 CFR �418.102, only a hospice medical director is authorized to admit a patient into hospice care. As such, the proposed bill could potentially lead to a violation of these federal requirements. Additionally, according to the Maine Board of Licensure in Medicine, any out-of-state physician must hold a valid Maine medical license for their orders to be recognized within the state.

While State Hospice Licensure Regulations do not directly address this specific issue, both CMS and state guidelines clearly require that any provider delivering direct care to hospice patients in Maine must be licensed in the state.

At this time, the Department of Licensing and Certification (DLC) has not received reports of any issues related to the ordering of hospice care.

Please feel free to contact me if you have any questions during your deliberation of this bill.

Sincerely,

Bill Montejo Director Division of Licensing and Certification Maine Department of Health and Human Services

RE: LD 1583 An Act Regarding Home Health Care and Hospice Services Ordered by a Health Care Provider Outside of Maine
Dear Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyers, and Members of the Committee:
The State Board of Nursing ("Board") licenses and regulates licensed practical nurses, registered professional nurses and advanced practice registered nurses in Maine. The Board is composed of 9 members - 5 actively practicing registered nurses, 1 actively practicing advanced practice registered nurse, 1 actively practicing licensed practical nurse and 2 public members. The Board's mission is to protect the public by licensing and regulating nurses, and approving prelicensure nursing education programs.
As written, this bill would allow a home health care or hospice provider, to deliver home health care or hospice services to a patient who resides in Maine based upon an order from a health care provider (advanced practice registered nurse) from another state or jurisdiction in the United States who is licensed and prescribes services pursuant to an in-person physical examination in the jurisdiction of licensure.
While the Board of Nursing (BON) appreciates the intent of the bill, the BON opposes the bill and has concerns for the following reasons:
1. The BON does not have jurisdiction over advanced practice registered nurses (APRNs) not licensed in Maine.

2. It is unclear how the requirement in sections 2145-A(1)(A) and 8641(1)(A), that the outof-state provider (APRN) be licensed and in good standing in another state will be enforced.

3. It is unclear how the requirement in sections 2145-A(1)(B) and 8641(1)(B), that the health care provider (APRN) must prescribe home health or hospice care services pursuant to an

If no contact and/or agreement is made, it is unclear if the out-of-state healthcare provider (APRN) will be involved in the patient's care after ordering the home health care or hospice services. Senator lngwersen, Representative Meyer, and honorable members of the Committee on Health
and Human Services, I am Representative Kristen Cloutier and I am here to present LD 1583, An

Act Regarding Home Health Care and Hospice Services Ordered by a Health Care Provider

Outside of Maine.

-

LD 1583 seeks to make a simple clarification in Maine law, so that providers of home care and
hospice services have complete confidence that they are operating fully within our state's
regulations.

Currently there are numerous instances in which Maine patients seek care in other states. For
instance, many people who live along the border with New Hampshire receive some of their health
care services in our neighboring state. In addition, many Mainers travel to Boston for specialty
care or due to a center-of-excellence relationship with their Maine-based provider.
The problem occurs when these patients retum home to their health care providers here in Maine. Current regulations in Maine are unclear and potentially contradictory with regard to whether
Maine-based providers are allowed to carry out orders from out-of-state physicians. This ambiguity creates confusion and hesitation, ultimately affecting the delivery of essential care to
patients in need.

While in some cases, primary care physicians (PCP) in Maine may be able to issue orders for
specialty care when their patient returns home, this is not always the case. A PCP may not have the
necessary expertise or familiarity with the patient's specific condition, and may recognize the liability present, and therefore may not be comfortable issuing such orders.
LD 1583 addresses this issue by providing clear guidelines for Maine providers to follow. By
allowing them to deliver home health care and hospice services based on orders from out-of-state physicians who have conducted an in-person physical examination, we can ensure that patients
receive the care they need in a timely and efficient manner.

District 94: Part of Lewiston

This issue was brought to me directly by Andwell, a home care and hospice provider in my
community. You will hear from them and others today who have direct experience with this issue and who can provide real life examples of how this problem interferes with the delivery of critical
health care services in our state.
LD 15 83 is not about changing the standard of care, but rather about providing clarity and
consistency in our regulations. Maine providers need to know that they are operating within the
law, and this bill provides them with the necessary guidance.
I urge you to support LD 1583, which will help to improve the delivery of home health care and
hospice services in our state. By doing so, we can ensure that patients receive the care they need,
and providers can operate with confidence and clarity.
Thank you. I am happy to answer any questions you may have, although I may defer to the providers offering testimony after me, who can speak to their own experiences.

The Maine Medical Association [MMA) is a professional organization representing over 4,000 physicians, residents, and medical students in Maine. .

We are grateful to our partners for determining a fix to ensure that clinicians can provide
necessary care to their patients and also ensuring they are not acting on orders that might expose them to legal or licensure risk. This bill addresses a challenge thatcomes up more
often than` you might expect, how can patients in Maine receive timely home health or

Across the state, Maine patients routinely receive care from out-of--state providers, especially in `border communities and through center-of-excellence programs for surgeries and specialty care. These are important and clinically sound provider-patient
relationships.

However, what comes next after receiving this out-of-state care has increasingly become a

concern. After receiving such care, many of these patients return home to Maine and

require follow-up services, such as home health or hospice, which would be delivered by

Maine-based providers. These services often rely on medical orders issued by the

out-of-state providers. But, under current Maine law, unless that out-of-state provider is

licensed here or holds a special registration for telemedicine, their orders may not be

considered valid.

� .

' --

LD 1583 provides a practical and patient-centered solution. It allows Maine home health
and hospice agencies to accept orders from licensed out-of-state providers, but with importantsafeguards. These safeguards include requiring that the provider must be
actively licensed a11d in good standing in their home jurisdiction, they must have
conducted an in-person physical examination in that jurisdiction, and if the patient has a Maine-based primary care provider, the out-of-state provider must make a good-faith effort to contact them in order to coordinate care.

These provisions ensure both access and accountability. They support timely and patient-centered care without undermining patient safety or Maine's regulatory oversight.

LD 1583 does not permit unregulated practice or undercut the role of Maine-licensed providers. Instead, it acknowledges the reality of contemporary healthcare and details clear, reasonable guardrails to ensure patients receive the care they need while keeping
Maine providers out of legal trouble.

Thank you for considering the thoughts of Maine's physicians, and we hope you support

LD 1583.

Re: LD 1583 - "An Act Regarding Home Health Care and Hospice Services Ordered by a Health Care Provider Outside of Maine"
Dear Senator Ingwerson, Representative Meyer and members of the Health and Human Services Committee:

Senator Ingwerson, Representative Meyer, and members of the Health and Human Services Committee, I am Tim Terranova, Executive Director of the Maine Board of Licensure in Medicine ("BOLIM"). I am submitting this letter in opposition to LD 1583.
The Maine Board of Licensure in Medicine ("BOLIM") licenses and regulates allopathic physicians and physician assistants in Maine. BOLIM is composed of 11 members: 6 physicians who actively practice medicine; 2 physician assistants who actively render medical services; and 3 public members. BOLIM's mission is to protect the public by ensuring its licensees are ethical, professional and competent. It fulfills this mission by licensing, regulating, and educating physicians and physician assistants.
BOLIM offers the following comments in opposition to LD 1583:

BOLIM's primary mission is to protect the public health and welfare of Maine citizens by ensuring that those licensed to practice medicine or render medical services in Maine are honest and competent practitioners. Although this bill seems straight forward and possibly common sense, it leaves Maine citizens vulnerable to the unregulated practice of medicine or rendering of medical services that may fall below the required standards of care.

It is the standard for physicians and physician assistants that patient care occurs where the patient is located. That is why those providers who provide patient care to patients located in Maine need to be licensed to practice medicine or render medical services by either BOLIM or the Board of Osteopathic Licensure. BOLIM, like any licensing board, only has jurisdiction over its licensees. The practice of medicine or the rendering of medical services can include the authorization or direction of care via orders that will be provided by other individuals.

Other states may conclude they do not have, or may choose not to exercise, jurisdiction over licensees who provide care to patients located outside their state.
Sections 2145-A, 1, A and 8641, 1, A of the bill requires the out-of-state provider to be licensed and in good standing in another state but provides no mechanism or standards for the Maine provider to follow to perform these verification tasks and does not specify how these provisions could be enforced. What standards are required to verify active licensure, how are Maine providers required to document this information, and what are the repercussions if these are not completed appropriately?
Sections 2145-A, 1, B and 8641, 1, B of the bill may be unenforceable. If the out-of-state provider has no Maine license or privilege, BOLIM has no jurisdiction over a professional living and practicing in a different state and therefore cannot ensure that the provider performed the in-person exam required by the bill, that they did so competently, and that their orders to the Maine provider(s) meet the required standards of care. How does the home health care or hospice provider ensure this type of evaluation has been completed, how is it documented and what are the repercussions for their license if it is not completed appropriately?
Likewise, sections 2145-A, 2 and 8641, 2, of the bill may be unenforceable. If the out-of-state provider has no Maine license or privilege, BOLIM has no jurisdiction over a professional living and practicing in a different state. How does the home health care or hospice provider ensure this type of contact with a primary care provider has been attempted or completed, how is it documented and what is the repercussions for their license if it is not completed appropriately? If this is not completed appropriately, the state has no jurisdiction or enforcement action available for the practitioner in the other state.
Relative to the practice of medicine of the rendering of medical services there are two key gaps in these bills that may leave patients unprotected. First, the out-of-state provider may not have performed the in-person exam required by the bill. Second, the provider may have issued orders for home health or hospice care that do not meet the standard of care but which practice of medicine or rendering of medical services may fall outside the jurisdiction of the Maine medical boards and outside the jurisdiction of the provider's state of licensure
The issues identified above mean that, if this bill were law and something were to go wrong, Maine patients might have no mechanism to protect themselves from incompetence or dishonest practitioners This bill creates a loophole that allows for the unregulated practice of medicine or rendering of medical services to patients within the state.
This very issue is the reason that compacts have been accepted by so many states. BOLIM is part of the Interstate Medical Licensure Compact (IMLC) which is for MDs and DOs. Since the IMLC started, Maine has seen its licensed physician population grow by more than 2,500. The vast majority of those licensees do not have a Maine address and are believed to be practicing via telemedicine. There is also a physician assistant compact adopted by the Legislature that, when it becomes operational, is expected to have the same proportional effect.
Although rare, the increase in the use of telehealth has seen some physicians or physician assistants attempt to practice medicine or render medical services at a standard of care below the minimum required standards of medical care necessary to safely and appropriately treat the patient. These issues have a direct impact on Maine patients and patient care and, because these individuals were required to have a Maine license, BOLIM has been able to take action to protect Maine patients.
